Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". BOOK NOTE: the guide says a nucleosome holds "a DNA segment of about 150 base pairs". NCERT gives 146 bp wrapped on the histone core, within a repeat of about 200 bp per nucleosome. The card gives 146 bp wrapped and notes the repeat, and records the guide's figure.

insider_note: Two numbers carry this answer: EIGHT histones and 146 base pairs. Write both in the first two lines.

steps.label: What a nucleosome is
steps.margin_note: Definition plus the packing problem it solves. Six lines.
lines: A NUCLEOSOME is the repeating, bead-like unit of
chromatin.
It consists of a core of histone proteins with
DNA wound around it.
Nucleosomes are how a two-metre length of DNA
is packed into a nucleus a few micrometres
across.
steps.why: Two metres of DNA has to fit inside a nucleus, and the nucleosome is the first and largest step of that packing.
common_mistakes: Calling a nucleosome a chromosome. It is the repeating UNIT of chromatin, far smaller.
Saying it is made only of DNA. It is DNA plus HISTONE PROTEIN.
steps.memory_tip: A bead of protein with DNA wound on it.

steps.label: The histone octamer
steps.margin_note: The count, the four histone names, the base pairs, and H1's position.
lines: The core is made of EIGHT histone molecules and
is called the HISTONE OCTAMER.
It is two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
About 146 BASE PAIRS of DNA are wound around
this octamer, in about 1.75 turns.
One more histone, H1, sits where the DNA enters
and leaves the bead.
steps.why: Two copies each of four histones is what makes eight, so the name octamer is the composition stated in one word.
common_mistakes: Saying the octamer includes H1. H1 is OUTSIDE the octamer, at the entry and exit point.
Giving the wrong count. It is EIGHT histones, two each of four kinds.
steps.memory_tip: Two of each of four kinds makes eight; H1 is the ninth, and it sits outside.

steps.label: Why the DNA winds on
steps.margin_note: Both charges, the two amino acids, and the attraction. Six lines.
lines: DNA is NEGATIVELY charged, because of its
phosphate groups.
Histones are POSITIVELY charged, because they
are rich in the basic amino acids LYSINE and
ARGININE.
So the DNA is held on the octamer by an
electrical attraction between opposite charges.
steps.why: Opposite charges attract, so the wrapping needs no energy and no enzyme — it happens because of what the two molecules are made of.
common_mistakes: Saying histones are acidic. They are BASIC, and that is what makes them positive.
Giving no reason for the winding. The charge attraction is this mark.
steps.memory_tip: Negative DNA on positive protein: opposites attract.

steps.label: Chromatin and beads on a string
steps.margin_note: Define chromatin, give the beads-on-a-string phrase, and name the microscope.

lines.text: Beads on a string, under the electron

lines: DNA together with histone proteins is called
CHROMATIN.
Nucleosomes are the repeating units of
chromatin.
Under the ELECTRON MICROSCOPE, chromatin looks
like BEADS ON A STRING: the nucleosomes are the
beads and the linker DNA is the string.
Further coiling of this gives the chromosome.
steps.why: The beads-on-a-string picture is what a nucleosome actually looks like, which is why the phrase is worth writing exactly.
common_mistakes: Saying the beads are seen under a light microscope. It is the ELECTRON microscope.
Confusing chromatin with chromosome. Chromatin coils further to give a chromosome.
steps.memory_tip: Beads are nucleosomes; the string is the linker DNA.

steps.label: Diagram — nucleosome
steps.margin_note: No diagram mark — the question says 'write briefly'. The bead is worth sketching because it fixes the 1.75 turns and H1's position in one picture.

elements.caption: Step 1 — the histone octamer, a ball of eight proteins
Step 2 — the DNA wound almost twice around it
Step 3 — the linker DNA running on to the next bead
Step 4 — the H1 histone where the DNA enters and leaves

steps.why: Drawing it shows the two facts the words have to carry separately: the DNA goes round more than once, and H1 sits exactly where it enters and leaves.
common_mistakes: Drawing the DNA passing through the octamer. It winds AROUND the outside.
Drawing one full turn. The DNA makes about 1.75 turns.
Drawing H1 inside the core. H1 sits OUTSIDE, at the entry and exit point.
steps.memory_tip: Round the outside, nearly twice, with H1 at the door.
